title: The Second Declension
description: Masculine and neuter nouns in -ος and -ον; cases, word order and movable ν.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html: Greek nouns change their endings for case: nominative for the subject, genitive for "of", dative for "to" or "for", accusative for the direct object, vocative for address. Because the case shows the job of each word, Greek word order is free: ἄνθρωπος βλέπει δοῦλον and δοῦλον βλέπει ἄνθρωπος both mean "a man sees a servant".

blocks.caption: λόγος and δῶρον
rows: Neuter nouns have the same form in the nominative and accusative. There is no indefinite article: λόγος is "a word".

blocks.caption: Accent of nouns
blocks.html: A noun keeps its accent on the syllable where the nominative has it, as far as the general rules allow; in the genitive and dative an accented ultima takes the circumflex: θεός, θεοῦ, θεῷ.

blocks.caption: How the course checks word order
blocks.html: You may type a Greek answer in any order of the right words, as long as no postpositive word (δέ, γάρ, οὖν) stands first and no article stands last; when your order differs from ours the feedback shows ours.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: λόγοι (nominative plural) and λόγους (accusative plural) differ only in the ending: read to the end of every word.
